title: SEO for a Winery Website | Craft Beer School
desc: SEO for a winery website: page structure for wines, vineyards and visits, local search for the cellar door, content ideas and common traps.
teaser: A winery site has more to say than most. The task is to organise it so that search engines and visitors both follow.
standfirst: A winery has two audiences: people who might buy wine and people who might visit. Good SEO treats them as separate journeys and gives each a clear path.
sections:
People search by wine, by place and by occasion. Build pages for each. A page per wine with grape, vintage, tasting notes and how to buy. A page for the estate or region that tells the story. A visit page covering tastings, tours, opening hours and how to book. An events page.

Avoid putting all wines on one long page. One topic per page makes it easier for a person to land on exactly what they wanted.

Each wine page should say what a visitor wants to know: grape variety, style, a plain tasting description, serving suggestions and where to buy. Write your own descriptions, not text pasted from a distributor. For vintage wines, keep an archive page and mark old vintages clearly, so people do not buy a wine that is gone.

Use clear names. If your wine has a fanciful name, add the grape and the style in the page title so that searchers who type those words find it.
The cellar door and local search

If you welcome visitors, set up a Google Business Profile as in our guide for a taproom, which applies equally to a tasting room. Make sure the address, hours and booking link match your website. Add directions and parking information, because a winery is often outside the town.

Add photos of the vineyard, the tasting room and the view. Check opening hours at harvest and festival times.

Write about things only you can explain: the vineyard, the harvest, the way a grape behaves in your climate. Real detail beats generic wine copy. A short, accurate piece on how the harvest unfolds each year will often serve readers better than a long piece about wine in general.

Keep claims honest. Do not make health claims. Do not describe wine in ways that encourage excess. See content that brings visitors.

Check the site on a phone, since many visitors are travelling. Compress photos so pages load quickly. If you use an age gate, make sure it does not stop search engines from reading the content. Test it. Submit a sitemap in Search Console and watch for errors there. Use structured data for your business and events if your developer can add it.

Rules for selling and shipping alcohol online vary by country and, in India, by state. Some places do not allow it. Check before you build a shop. If you cannot sell online, make the page say where to buy and let people enquire.

Visits are the part of a winery that search can bring directly. Give each regular offer its own page: a tasting, a tour, a harvest day, a lunch. State duration, group size, what is included and how to book, in text. Add a booking button that works on a phone. Keep dates current. Remove past events or mark them clearly.

Think about those who cannot drink. Mention non-alcoholic options, tours of the vineyard and food, so that groups with drivers or non-drinkers see a reason to come. Remind visitors about arranging safe travel home. It is the right thing to do and it keeps your listing honest about what a visit is.

Tie it back to measurement: count how many booking requests come from search compared with your other routes, as set out in measuring website leads.

Add a short page of practical details for visitors: how long the drive is from the nearest town, whether the road is suitable for all vehicles, whether there is shade and seating and whether children and pets are welcome. These are the questions people really ask before they set out.

Ask a friend who has never visited to find your tasting booking page from a phone. Where they stumble is where visitors stumble.

Photograph the last stretch of the approach road, so a first-time visitor recognises the turning.

Do not stuff pages with repeated place names. Do not buy links. Do not copy another winery's descriptions. Keep it honest and useful. Give it time. For other common errors, see SEO mistakes drinks websites make.
faqs: Not necessarily. A few well-written pages about your estate, harvest and visits can do more than a blog nobody updates.
Can search find my wine club?
Yes if it has its own page, a clear name and a way to sign up. Describe what members receive and when.
Does the vintage in the page title help?
It can help people looking for that vintage. Update or archive pages as vintages sell out.
